lesson.title: How Surprised Should You Be? Defining the P-Value
lesson.summary: The p-value is the probability, computed by assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, and it is the single most important number a hypothesis test produces.
lesson.body:
Here is the definition, stated precisely because getting it exactly right matters more than almost anything else in this unit: a p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic, or sample result, at least as extreme as the one you actually got, computed under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that your result happened by some vague notion of chance. It is a conditional probability, the probability of this data given that H0 is true, and because it starts by assuming H0 is true, it can never turn around and tell you the probability that H0 itself is true. That would require a completely different kind of information, such as a prior probability, which classical hypothesis testing does not use.

Once you have a test statistic like z = negative 2.00, the p-value is simply the area under the standard normal curve in the tail or tails beyond that value, the same kind of area you already know how to find with normal probability calculations. A small p-value means the observed result would be rare if H0 were true, so the data are hard to reconcile with H0. A large p-value means the observed result would be unremarkable if H0 were true, so the data are perfectly consistent with H0, though this never proves H0 is true, it only means the data failed to contradict it.

Back to the cereal boxes: the test statistic was z = negative 2.00 for a two-sided test of H0: mu = 16 against Ha: mu is not equal to 16. The two-sided p-value is 2 times the area to the left of negative 2.00 under the standard normal curve, which is 2 times 0.0228, or 0.0456. Put into words with the correct conditional logic: if the machine truly fills boxes at a mean of 16 ounces, there is about a 4.56 percent chance that a random sample of 36 boxes would produce a sample mean at least as far from 16, in either direction, as 15.9 ounces, just from ordinary sampling variability. That 4.56 percent is small, not impossible, but small enough to raise real suspicion that H0 might not be true.

Exactly how you compute that tail area, whether the test is one-sided or two-sided, is the mechanical skill covered next. Deciding how small a p-value has to be before you actually act on that suspicion is a separate question, covered in the significance level and statistical significance chapters that follow.
